Free boundaries tools

20 short exercises on boundaries, 2 to 7 minutes each, free and with no account needed. Open one and it runs right in the page.

The 20 tools

  • How easily you say no

    Set a dial for how comfortable you are saying no in different parts of your life. Most people find it varies more than they expected.

    Dials · 4 min

  • Yes, no, or maybe

    Sort the requests and obligations currently on you into a real yes, a real no, and a maybe. Then look at how many of your yeses were actually maybes.

    Sorter · 5 min

  • Boundary phrases you would actually say

    Build a short set of phrases for declining, delaying, and holding a line, in words that sound like you rather than like a script.

    Plan builder · 5 min

  • Where you overextend

    Rate how often a set of overextending habits has been true lately: saying yes on reflex, apologizing for needs, doing the emotional work for everyone.

    Reflection · 5 min

  • The signs you said yes when you meant no

    Tick the after-the-fact signals you recognize from times you agreed to something you did not want. These show up before the resentment does, and they are easier to catch.

    Noticing list · 3 min

  • When they push back

    Turn over the lines people use when you hold a boundary, from guilt trips to "just this once", and see what is happening underneath and what you could say without folding.

    Perspective cards · 5 min

  • Who asks, and who you can't refuse

    Place the people who make requests of you on a grid of how often they ask against how hard it is to say no to them. Two of the corners are where your time actually disappears.

    Grid · 6 min

  • The line that keeps moving

    Trace one boundary you have set before and watched slide: how it was drawn, how it eroded, and what it would take to hold it. Most lines do not get crossed all at once.

    Guided writing · 7 min

  • What you are afraid a no will cost

    Choose the fears that come up when you consider saying no, then rank them. Seeing the actual fear makes it possible to check whether it is true.

    Card pick · 5 min

  • Which lines are easiest to hold

    Rank kinds of boundaries from easiest to hardest for you to keep: your time, your body, your money, your phone, your opinions, your privacy. Your order says a lot about where you were taught you had a say.

    Ranking · 4 min

  • What your yeses are made of

    Divide 100 points across the reasons you say yes, from genuinely wanting to, to avoiding a fight, to reflex. The bars show how much of your agreement is actually agreement.

    Budget · 4 min

  • When your time stops being yours

    Mark the times of the week when other people's needs take over your time: the after-hours messages, the drop-ins, the calls you always answer. A pattern usually appears.

    Week map · 3 min

  • Seven days of yes and no

    Each evening, rate how much of the day felt like yours, how many things you agreed to that you did not want, and how you felt after any no you managed to say. A week of this shows where the leaks are.

    7-day log · 2 min

  • The pause before you answer

    A four-minute exercise for the moment someone asks you for something. Practice it with a recent request so the pause is there when the next one arrives.

    Guided exercise · 5 min

  • Whose job is it

    Sort a list of things people carry into mine, theirs, and shared. Many of the heaviest things we carry were never ours to pick up.

    Sorter · 5 min

  • Your plan for the next family visit

    Build a small plan for a visit home or a family gathering: how long you will stay, what you will not discuss, what you will do when it gets hard, and how you will land afterwards.

    Plan builder · 6 min

  • How you take other people's no

    Boundaries run both ways. Rate how often you keep pushing after someone has said no, read into "I'm busy", or show up when you were not invited. Most people have never looked at this side of it.

    Reflection · 5 min

  • How reachable you let yourself be

    Set a dial for how available you are through your phone and screens: work messages after hours, group chats, reply speed, notifications at night. Availability is a boundary most people never set on purpose.

    Dials · 4 min

  • Work boundaries worth a look

    Tick the things you do at work or school that quietly hand your time, credit, or energy to other people. None of them is a big deal on its own. Together they add up to a job you did not sign up for.

    Noticing list · 3 min

  • Write the message, then cut it in half

    Draft a boundary message to someone, then take it through four edits: strip the apology, strip the excuse, keep the warmth, check the ask. What is left is usually shorter, kinder, and clearer.

    Guided writing · 7 min

What these tools are, and are not

Every tool here is free and works without an account: choose cards, move dials, sort a list, follow a paced breath, or keep a seven-day log, and read back what you noticed at the end. They are built to make a vague feeling more specific, which is often the first useful step.

None of them diagnoses, screens for or treats anything, and nothing you see at the end is a score or a label. If something you notice worries you, a licensed therapist is the right next conversation, and the directory is free to browse.
